newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope visits child cancer ward as hospital stay ends.
newsitem.headline: Pope visits child cancer ward as hospital stay ends.

text.p: Pope John Paul on Tuesday comforted children suffering from cancer, some of them terminally ill, before he was due to leave hospital and return to the Vatican to continue his convalescence from an appendix operation.
The 76-year-old Pontiff, who was due to leave the Gemelli hospital at about 1600 GMT, spent about 30 minutes visiting sick children in the cancer ward next to his 10th floor suite.
A number of the children, whom the Pope caressed during the visit, were bald from chemotherapy. About 10 of the 30 children in the ward are considered terminally ill.
"The Pope asked me how old I was and blessed me," Vincenzo Valentini, 11, told reporters after the visit.
Vincenzo had received a bone marrow transplant from his sister and was in hospital for a check-up.
"The children were thrilled to see him," said Vincenzo's father Settimo. "He had a kind word for everyone."
Francesco Lo Re, a three-year-old boy who has a brain tumour, gave the Pope flowers as his mother held back tears.

"These kids have a tremendous will to live," she told reporters. "This gives me hope. The will of the Lord will be done. Either my boy will get well or the Lord will give us enough strength to go through with it," she said.

Brief footage of the visit shot by Vatican Television showed the Pope in relatively good form as he greeted the children. He entered the ward with a cane but stood unassisted as he gave each of the children and their parents rosaries.
The young patients had sent the Pope a note, signed "the children next door", asking him to visit before he left the hospital.
The Pope entered the Gemelli on October 6. He had surgery last Tuesday to remove an inflamed appendix which doctors said had caused several fevers and abdominal pain since December.
They said the surgery confirmed that there had been no recurrence of a colon tumour removed in 1992.

Doctors removed stitches from the operation on Tuesday and have ordered the Pope to rest. His next public appearance is due on Sunday, when he will recite his weekly prayer and address from the window of his apartments overlooking St Peter's Square.

The Vatican has not excluded the possibility that the Pope will make a brief appearance from the window on Wednesday, the 18th anniversary of his election in 1978 as the first non-Italian Pope in 455 years.

Doctors who have treated the Pope for the appendix have not, however, addressed another problem -- a violently trembling left hand which media reports have suggested is caused by Parkinson's disease or a related neurological disorder.
The Vatican has not denied a string of reports in recent months that the Pope is suffering from the disease.
